title: Women's sports
description: Sports participated by women and girls
wiki_lead:
The participation of women and girls in sports, physical fitness, and exercise has existed throughout history. However, participation rates and activities vary in accordance with nation, era, geography, and stage of economic development.
Until roughly 1870, women's activities tended to be informal and recreational in nature, lacked rules codes, and emphasized physical activity rather than competition. Today, women's sports are more sport-specific and have developed into both amateur levels and professional levels in various places internationally, but is found primarily within developed countries where conscious organization and accumulation of wealth has occurred. In the mid-to-latter part of the 20th century, female participation in sport and the popularization of their involvement increased, particularly during its last quarter. Very few organized sports have been invented by women. Sports such as Newcomb ball, netball, acrobatic gymnastics, and tumbling, and possibly stoolball, are examples.
Women's involvement in sports is more visible in well-developed countries and today their level of participation and performance still varies greatly by country and by sport. Despite an increase in women's participation in sport, the male demographic is still the larger of the two. These demographic differences are observed globally. Female dominated sports are the one exception. Girls' participation in sports tends to be higher in the United States than in other parts of the world like Western Europe and Latin America. Girls' participation in more violent contact sports is far less than that of their male counterparts.
Two important divisions exist in relation to female sporting categories. These sports either emerged exclusively as an organized female sport with male exclusion or were developed as an organized female variant of a sport first popularized by a male demographic and therefore became a female category. In all but a few exceptional cases, such as in the case of camogie, a female variant, or "women's game" uses the same name of the sport popularly played by men, but is classified into a different category which is differentiated by sex: men's or women's, or girls or boys. Female variants are widely common while organized female sports by comparison are rare and include team sports such as netball, throwball, artistic (née synchronized) swimming, and ringette. In female sports, the supposed benefits of gender parity, gender equity and sex segregation are controversial.
Except in a few rare cases like women's professional tennis, professional women's sport rarely provide competitors with a livable income. In addition, competing for media coverage of the women's variant of a sport which is primarily popular among males, creates complex barriers. More recently, there has been an increasing amount of interest, research, investment and production in regards to equipment design for female athletes. Interest and research involving the identification of sex-specific injuries, particularly though not exclusively among high performance female athletes, has increased as well, such as in the case of concussions and the female athlete triad, a.k.a. "Relative energy deficiency in sport" (RED-S).
At times female athletes have engaged in social activism in conjunction with their participation in sport. Protest methods have included playing strikes, social media campaigns, and in the case of America, federal lawsuits on grounds of inequality, usually as it relates to gender parity principles, American law and Title IX which demand schools that any funds given to support students' sports should be equally distributed between boys and girls. Public service oriented promotional campaigns for girls in sport involve a variety of media campaign styles.

History


Ancient civilizations

Before each ancient Olympic Games a separate women's athletic event was held at the stadium in Olympia, called the Heraean Games and dedicated to the goddess Hera.
grok_lead: Women's sports encompass organized athletic competitions designated exclusively for female participants, segregated from male categories to ensure competitive fairness given the profound physiological advantages males typically hold in strength, speed, power, and endurance due to sex-based differences in skeletal muscle mass, bone density, cardiovascular capacity, and hormonal influences driven by sex chromosomes and testosterone exposure. These disparities result in performance gaps of approximately 10-12% in aerobic events like distance running and 30-50% in anaerobic strength tasks, rendering mixed-sex competition inequitable for females in most disciplines. Historically, female athletic participation was limited in ancient civilizations, with rare exceptions such as the Heraean Games in Greece honoring Hera, where women competed in footraces clad in chitons; systematic segregation and promotion emerged in the modern era, beginning with women's debut at the 1900 Paris Olympics in events like tennis and golf, though full inclusion lagged due to prevailing views on female frailty. Expansion accelerated post-World War II, with milestones including the addition of women's track events at the 1928 Amsterdam Olympics and the establishment of international federations; in the United States, the 1972 enactment of Title IX prohibited sex discrimination in federally funded education, catalyzing a surge in female collegiate sports participation from under 30,000 to over 200,000 athletes within a decade. Today, women's sports feature professional leagues across soccer, basketball, tennis, and emerging disciplines like ringette, alongside global events such as the FIFA Women's World Cup, which drew over 1 billion viewers in 2019, reflecting growing commercial viability and cultural recognition despite persistent funding disparities relative to men's counterparts. Notable achievements include feats like Serena Williams ' 23 Grand Slam singles titles in tennis and Katie Ledecky's dominance in swimming, underscoring female excellence within sex-segregated frameworks. A defining controversy involves the inclusion of transgender womenâbiological males who transition after puberty âin female categories, where empirical studies indicate retention of significant advantages in strength and speed even after testosterone suppression, as evidenced by higher handgrip strength and push-up capacity compared to cisgender females, prompting debates over policy reforms to preserve category integrity based on biological sex rather than gender identity. This issue highlights tensions between inclusion and fairness, with causal analyses prioritizing immutable sex-based traits over social constructs in high-stakes competition.
